digitWords.note: Already in the rule on every platform. un and una stay out: they are articles.

spokenNumbers.note: PROPOSED rule change, on every platform: today a spoken word adds one digit and only single digit words count. Spanish speakers often say a phone number in pairs and hundreds (cuatro cero cuatro, quinientos cincuenta y cinco, cero uno, cuarenta y dos). A group is a hundreds word with the tens and units after it, or a tens or teen word with the unit after it, or a unit word alone: it adds 3 digits when it starts with a hundreds word (doscientos treinta y cuatro is 234, one group of 3), 2 when it starts with a tens or teen word (treinta y dos), and 1 for a unit word. y joins a tens word, including veinte and diez in the split spellings veinte y dos and diez y seis, to the unit after it. un and una count only right after such a y (treinta y un, cuarenta y una); alone they are articles. mil is not a number word here, so a spoken year (dos mil veintiséis) never builds a run. Words are listed folded (no accents), as the rule folds a note before matching.

months.note: Twin of the English month-name date: a run beside a month name stays a date (19 de noviembre de 2026). de may sit between the day, the month and the year.
months.question: mar (sea) and may are also other words; the short forms count only right before or after digits, as the English short months do.

streetWords.note: Twin of the English street words: a number written right after or before one of these is an address, not a phone number (calle Maple 412, avenida 5).

radio: On the radio, read a phone number back digit by digit (seis, siete, ocho), never in pairs: sesenta and setenta, and dos and doce, are easy to mishear.
